div.p: We present an approach to utilising unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as communication relays, in which a dynamic positioning algorithm drives UAVs automatically to achieve the best incoming and outgoing signal strength and packet throughput among participating ground nodes. This approach can be applied to real-life scenarios with widely distributed communicating nodes, for example, disasters like earthquakes with damaged communication towers, and harvesting sensor readings from distributed sensor nodes.

UAVs can establish a direct communication link between multiple nodes if they are within communication ranges to the UAVs. If this is not possible, the UAVs may be scheduled to bridge communications between the nodes with some time delay. In other words, a delay tolerant network (DTN) among participating nodes can be formed whereby the UAVs fly over the nodes to collect, buffer and deliver data. This is useful in scenarios such as harvesting data from a widely distributed sensor network (e.g., flood monitoring in jungle).

We provide a scheduling analysis framework to show if a UAV can cover a given set of distributed nodes. Each sensor node may have a different priority, required frequency of visits and communication range. The framework was inspired by the response-time analysis approach for scheduling tasks in the real-time scheduling literature. In essence, we analyse the worst-case response time and schedulability for a UAV to visit and process communication requests for the lowest priority node among the participants.
We also demonstrate that this approach can interact with a physics simulator that models wind speed and turbulence, and learn and optimise on possible routes and positions for UAVs.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In recent years, the use of lightweight, flexible unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has been a popular idea in diverse applications ranging from surveillance missions to rare animal tracking. UAVs can be equipped with various antenna technologies, GPS, video cameras, infra-led cameras among others and can be deployed to incidents fast whilst flying at low altitudes. This ability has motivated us to consider utilising UAVs as communication relays in scenarios such as cost-effective data harvesting in a widely distributed sensor network (e.g., flood monitoring in jungles) as well as in the event of emergences (such as earthquakes, fires, and military operations and other disasters), where parts of the communication infrastructure could be damaged and it is difficult to recover them within a short period of time, and hence no direct communication between nodes is possible. In such applications, UAVs can be used to extend the communication range of remaining facilities in order for ground-based nodes to communicate with those that are not in direct contact.

This paper investigates the problem of quickly positioning UAVs in such aforementioned application areas. In particular, we present our work on enabling UAVs to maximise communication quality by dynamically manoeuvring to a position where the packet delivery rate and signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) between participants are maximised. UAVs may be deployed from different positions, and eventually will find a position by constantly searching for the balance in SNR(s) and packet throughputs of participating nodes. A PID controller is used for each communication path to drive the UAV in the correct direction, meaning that the bigger the control error is (i.e., the difference in SNR and packet throughput), the faster the UAV moves towards an optimal position.

In doing so, we have discovered an interesting behaviour that, if an area consisting of multiple ground-based nodes cannot be covered by a single UAV (or a limited number of UAVs) to establish direct communication links through the relay, it is still possible to set up a form of delay tolerant network (DTN) for the given area. In such scenarios, the UAV will circulate among the nodes to buffer and deliver packets. This DTN-like behaviour may not be suitable for real-time voice communications, but may be still worthwhile for (push-to-talk voice) messaging or text/data driven communications, where a few minutes of delay is usually tolerable. In this regard, we provide a scheduling analysis framework and an illustration to show if a UAV can cover a given set of distributed nodes, which is inspired by the response-time analysis approach for scheduling real-time tasks in the real-time scheduling literature.
The scope and contributions of the paper are as follows;
• A dynamic, optimising algorithm for positioning UAVs to establish the best communication quality,

• Application of the control theory (i.e., a PID controller per communication path) to drive UAVs in bridging communications in order to maximise the signal-to-noise (SNR) ratio and packet throughput among participants,

• Formation of a priority-based delay tolerant network (DTN) among participating nodes that cannot establish direct communication links using a UAV, and the development of a framework for scheduling visits of a UAV and the worst-case response time analysis,
• Integration with a realistic physics simulation model that reflects the actual position of each UAV in the presence of a varying degree of wind, turbulences, and other physical conditions.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to analyse the schedulability of UAVs using the real-time analysis techniques and use the PID controller algorithm to

div.head: Scheduling UAVs to Bridge Communications in Delay-Tolerant
div.p: Networks Using Real-Time Scheduling Analysis Techniques position UAVs. This paper is organised as follows. Section 2 briefly presents the system model used in this paper. Section 3 will discuss the dynamic positioning algorithm for bridging communications while Section 4 will present our scheduling analysis framework for delay-tolerant networks. Some simulation details will be given in Section 5. Limitations of our approach are given in Section 6. We draw a few conclusions and discuss future work in Section 7.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We assume that there are a set of UAVs available for use in bridging communications between a set of mobile and/or ground nodes spread over a certain area, which is characterised as a grid space (e.g., 1x1m initially). The number of UAVs and participating nodes can vary dynamically. In other words, the system model consists of
• At least one or multiple cooperating UAVs that are possibly deployed from various locations,

• A set of functional ground and/or mobile nodes in an area with varying communication ranges characterised by their radio models. We make the following assumptions, some of which may be possible to relax in the near future.
• A grid space of 1x1 metre for measuring and evaluating SNRs for different locations in a map,
• The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is measurable for each participating node (i.e., for each node, the SNR to and from a UAV is measured and an SNR map is constructed),
• Packet throughputs, i.e., the number of packets successfully delivered to a UAV from each ground station per second are available,
• The use of a simple waypoint mobility model for UAVs' movement,
• The availability of the radio propagation model for each wireless network technology and antenna used,

• The locations of all nodes are known, When attempting to bridge communications, the UAV can obtain the SNR values of packets from/to each participating node in the presence of a realistic, user-configurable radio propagation model, and is able to calculate the packet throughput for successfully delivered packets between nodes and each UAV.

div.head: III. DYNAMIC UAV POSITIONING ALGORITHM FOR BRIDGING COMMUNICATIONS A. THE PID-CONTROLLER BASED GREEDY ALGORITHM
div.p: The algorithm we describe below instructs each UAV to move towards or away from certain participating nodes in order to achieve the best communication quality for a given set of nodes. One of the key goals of the algorithm is to reduce the time it takes to establish communication links between nodes (hence, the use of a PID controller to drive a UAV). More specifically, the optimising criteria that we use to position UAVs are as follows.

• The SNRs (Signal-to-Noise Ratios) of packets from and to each participating node to be equally balanced whilst maximising the combined SNRs for packets between nodes and the UAV on a communication path.
• The packet throughputs for successfully delivered packets between participating nodes to be balanced.

• Bit error rates (BER) can also be measured if required The algorithm in Figure 1 attempts to find a place where the average SNR values of packets from and to different sources become close to the same, meaning that the communication relay is not biased towards any particular node in terms of SNRs and stays exactly where needed the most. In general, the UAV may fly at the lowest possible altitude unless there are obstacles or it has reached the best SNR on the given altitude and is trying to test SNR at different altitudes. The SNR values may be aged over time with an expiration time limit (e.g., exponential smoothing).

In doing so, we use the SNRs and packet throughputs as input to a PID controller for each communication path, which calculates the UAV's next waypoints. This means that the bigger the control errors, the faster the UAV will move to its next waypoint. The control errors are defined as follows in this context;
• Packet throughput control error = the difference in packet throughput for communications between the UAV and each participating node on a single communication path where the UAV is used as a relay,
• SNR control error = the difference in average SNR for packets delivered to and from the UAV on a single communication path.
In essence, the algorithm instructs the UAV to move on either x or y axis by MAX( PIDcal(Throughput), PIDcal(SNRs)) in order to make the greatest impact as early as possible.

The algorithm in Figure 1 records the average SNR values for each grid cell as the UAV moves around. Unless the UAV has regular periodic messages to deliver, it sends out echo request messages to all nodes involved at a regular interval. Upon receiving a returning packet with an SNR above a preset threshold, the UAV will move towards a node whose SNR value is lower using the PID controller's output. If it does not receive any packet in return from any participating node, it will keep moving towards the node that has not 978-1-4799-6944-9/14/$31.00 ©2014 IEEE responded assuming it is out of communication range. In such cases the control error will be large, meaning that the PID controller's output will make the UAV move fast, and the UAV will keep sending echo request message to the node in question. As soon as it receives a response with a valid SNR and packet throughput, the PID controller will make judgements as to how fast the UAV should move.

The UAV will keep manoeuvring until the number of packets arriving from all participating nodes will balance out at one point with the SNR values from the nodes being more or less the same -reaching the most advantageous position for a communication relay in terms of the SNR and packet throughputs. In general, the greater the number of deployed UAVs is, the higher the coverage and performance will be.

div.head: IV.FORMATION OF A PRIORITY-BASED DELAY TOLERANT NETWORK USING A UAV AND SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: When two or more nodes are out of direct communication range even with the available UAV(s), such UAVs can fly around to collect, buffer and deliver packets between the participating nodes. This is possible when the quality of service requirement is manageable (i.e., schedulable) and visits are made at a regular frequency (or driven by some kind of a priority mechanism with periods). This can be seen as a real-time scheduling problem and it is possible to test the schedulability or response times for a given set of nodes and UAVs.

div.head: CATEGORISATION
div.p: First, we have categorised some of the possible cases for one UAV and a number of nodes, which can be extended for multiple UAVs.

Starting with the simplest case as shown above in Figure 2 (Case 1), direct communication may be established using one UAV. The UAV will move between the two nodes to balance the SNRs and packet throughputs from and to each of the nodes.

In the second case, as in Figure 3, there is no direct communication link between two nodes and the UAV will fly back and forth between the nodes in order to collect, buffer and deliver data. This is a simple case in which the UAV only needs to find the signal strength and packet throughput for each grid or position it flies over. Once the required thresholds for signal strength and packet throughput are reached, the UAV can begin to collect or transmit data for a required amount of time or number of packets. If there are variances between visits in the amount of data to transfer or time to hover on a particular node, we may only consider the worst case for the purpose of the response time or schedulability analysis. Hence, the smaller the variances are, the more accurate such analyses will be overall.

Interesting problems arise when there are more than two nodes and a subset of them can be covered by a UAV simultaneously. For instance, in Case 3 in Figure 4 as illustrated above, the UAV may need to fly to node 1 through 3 one by one. Alternatively, the UAV may only need to visit Node 1 and 2 in turn if the radio ranges of Node 2 and 3 overlap with each other and can communicate with each other because the UAV's wireless comm range can reach Node 3 through Node 2. Or, the UAV can take only Route 3 to communicate with Node 2 and 3 simultaneously, leaving Route 2 obsolete in either cases. The cost of taking Route 1 and 3 may be different, and in this case, taking Route 1 may incur a shorter travel time for the UAV (assuming data from Node 3 are relayed instantly through Node 2 upon request, and wind and other physical conditions are the same), and hence is a better scheduling strategy. If, however, there is strong head/tail wind on Route 1, preventing the UAV to fly slowly, it would be beneficial to reschedule and take Route 3 instead. Such decisions can be made dynamically by considering the current physical circumstances, which we will show in the next section by interacting with a physics simulator called QRSim [4].

Here, we have discovered a few optimisation criteria; Finding a position with the best possible combined SNR and throughput (i.e., Position 1 in Case 5) is one of the key challenges in scheduling a UAV. Our approach relies on the PID controller based algorithm introduced earlier that drives a UAV between nodes in order to find a position where the SNR value and packet throughput for each direction of communication path become balanced. The UAV can remember that position, to which it may fly over directly on the next subsequent visits. This will save the overall travel time and, hence, improve the schedulability, response times, and/or area coverage.
However, if there is an imbalance in the required bandwidths for Node 2 and 3, the UAV may hover closer to one particular node to obtain a better signal strength or packet throughput for that node.

div.head: UAV SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: One of the goals of this paper is to provide a schedulability analysis framework determining whether a UAV can cover a set of nodes that are characterised by their priorities, communication times, distances from other nodes (travelling time or cost), required frequency of visits (periods), and deadlines.

Inspired by the well-known response time analysis in the real-time literature [1,2], we apply the same technique to analyse the worst-case response time for the lowest priority node, which is the sum of the computation times and blocking times of all higher priority nodes plus its own computation time. If the response time for the lowest priority node is within the deadline for the same node, it is said that the whole nodes in the group can be schedulable with the given UAV. This is for nodes with statically assigned priorities, hence, the following analogies. For instance, assume there are three nodes as shown in the example in Figure 7, and each of them is assigned a static priority depending on the criticality, value or importance of the messages to be received and delivered to that particular node.

div.head: DISCUSSIONS
div.p: The goals of the presented approach in general are 1) obtaining the worst-case response time to be able to test the schedulability for the given UAVs to cover a set of participating nodes, 2) serving as many nodes as possible by one UAV, and, 3) designing and implementing the UAV scheduler and to integrate in a network simulator, such as ns-3 [3]. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first to analyse schedulability of UAVs, apart from commercial examples like [5], whose techniques are not well known. Bearing this in mind, we have the following discussion points.

• The worst-case response time at any given position for a UAV is defined by initially by the starting position of the UAV. However, for the worst-case, we may consider rather pessimistic results of the response-time analysis.

div.p: • We assume the UAV knows where the nodes in a group are, what their communication requirements are in terms of periods or frequencies of visit, maximum communication times, and travel times.

• The heading direction or angle of UAVs often affects the communication times needed and link quality when the UAV is in contact with a node and trying to move towards the next node, and may lengthen or shorten the travel time.

• The response time analysis can be pessimistic as a UAV can serve more than one node concurrently (which is one of the limitations of the approach outlined above), and must be extended to deal with multiple UAVs. In order words, while a UAV is travelling it can serve more than one node, i.e., the UAV is opportunistically parallel processing communication requests. Hence, the communication times for closely located nodes whose communication ranges overlap may be reduced. We outline some of the possible improvement strategies below.

div.head: Improvement Strategies -Dealing with overlapping cases
div.p: In the Case 3, 4 and 5 above, some of the nodes can be served concurrently whilst a UAV is flying nearby two separate nodes. This means that the response time can be further reduced for the given nodes and the UAV may be able to handle more nodes. Hence, finding nodes that can be served simultaneously and instructing the UAVs to fly on a new path to a new imaginary waypoint that minimises the communication and travel time is important. The original remaining blocking time can be nullified as soon as UAV is in a viable/required communication range.

The blocking time for a communication/travel path is calculated as follows, where Dist stands for the distance between two nodes, MVCR the maximum viable communication range between a node and a UAV, and S the speed of the given UAV.

For instance, if the distance between two nodes is 10m, the UAV's speed 5m/s, and the MVCRs for Node 1 and 2 are both 2m, the blocking (i.e., travelling and noncommunicating) time is 1.2s, because ! Based on this observation, we can create a new path leading to a position where the UAV can serve more than one node at the same time. In fact, we can come up with multiple positions on the grid space that quality as the MVCRs for nodes that can be served simultaneously by one UAV. But, among all of them, the one that results in the shortest blocking or travel time will be selected as the new shortest path and new waypoint position to serve a particular set of nodes. Hence, this problem can be broken down into 1) deciding which neighbouring nodes can be served together (i.e., overlapping nodes in terms of MVCRs either directly or indirectly with the help of a UAV), and 2) finding a waypoint to serve a given set of nodes that minimises the distance the UAV has to travel from its current position.

For the first problem, it can be said that two nodes overlap each other directly in terms of communication range if the MVCR(node1) + MVCR(node2) > Dist(node1, node2). In addition, even if two nodes do not overlap directly, they can be served simultaneously if MCVR(node1) + MVCR(node2) + 2MVCR(UAV) > Dist(node1, node2).

It must take into account the UAV's MVCR to come up with the area.

For the second problem, i.e., finding the shortest path from the UAV's current position to a waypoint where multiple neighbouring nodes can be served together, we need to know where the UAV is located dynamically, and then calculate the nearest waypoint on the grid space out of a set of possible candidates. The current location of UAV affects the decision.

div.head: Runtime Scheduler Design
div.p: The response time analysis alone does not tell how nodes should be scheduled or how UAVs should move at runtime. Rather, it assumes the worst case scenario where all nodes are activated simultaneously (i.e., the critical instance [2]), and determines whether a set of nodes are schedulable by a UAV. For this reason, we need a runtime scheduler that actually manages the UAV's movements among the participating nodes -a scheduler deployed on a UAV; we briefly describe the key algorithm and high-level implementation details.

Runtime Scheduling Criteria Scheduling criteria are dynamically determined by There are a few priority assignment strategies in the literature for real-time systems. The most common and widely known is the rate monotonic priority assignment technique [1], which assigns the highest priority to ones that are executed most frequently (i.e., with the shortest period). In the case of scheduling UAVs over distributed nodes, this means assigning higher priorities to those that require more frequent visits. One variation to this is the deadline monotonic priority assignment technique, which assigns a higher priority to a more urgent task. It is also possible to assign priorities according to the value or importance of the data to receive. Priorities may change at runtime if there are dynamic changes in the number of nodes or UAVs, or in the scheduling requirements. For such scenarios, the earliestdeadline-first (EDF) or other dynamic scheduling frameworks can also be used -however, statically determining the worst-case response time would be impossible in such cases.

div.head: V. IMPLEMENTATION AND SIMULATION
div.p: We have implemented the algorithm and example cases in the ns-3 [3] In the figure above, the fluctuating red-line illustrates the location of the UAV on the x-axis, overshooting slightly due to the PID-controller output, but eventually balancing out. The SNRs for packets to and from each access points (i.e., ground stations) as well as the total number of packets received are shown. Notice that the numbers of packets delivered climb constantly as the UAV is trying to reach an optimal position between two nodes (node 3 and 4 in the example). The SNR values are not clearly visible in the figure due to different scales (see the bottom), but they also fluctuate as the UAV is nearing the point where they balance out eventually.

div.head: VI. LIMITATIONS
div.p: The worst-case response time analysis is pessimistic, but some improvement strategies are suggested in the discussions section.

The characterisation of nodes, i.e., by period, communication time, and so on may be limiting in real-life. There may extra considerations or preferences to take into account (and other importance parameters).

In addition, the actual physical radio environment may be imperfect and should be investigated. It is also necessary to deal with interferences; we have used a simple jamming model in ns-3 for now -one that ignores the collision detection and broadcasts a lengthy packet periodically.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, we presented an approach to utilising UAVs as communication relays and discussed different cases and ways to position them to maximise the communication efficiency. It is also possible to create a delay tolerant network and we have shown how one could analyse the schedulability of a set of nodes by means of the responsetime analysis from the real-time literature. We have demonstrated how this approach could interact with a physics simulator to better reflect physical elements and dynamically optimise the speed and routes of UAVs.

As part of the future work, we plan to devise a formal model-checking approach to determine whether a set of given nodes are schedulable or if not, how many UAVs are required to make them schedulable. We are also interested in dealing with moving targets or nodes, and using the speed of the objects and directions to better predict possible waypoints of UAVs. It may be possible to employ multiple UAVs and assign them groups of nodes to serve. For a large number of nodes that cannot be covered by one UAV, it is necessary to cluster nodes into smaller subgroups, so that a UAV can each serve a group of nodes.
There are a number of strategies for grouping nodes, depending on the following criteria;
• Required frequency of visits to nodes • Distance and travel times between nodes • Communication overheads
